summary: On Aug 12, the Labor Department reported consumer prices rose 3.4% in July from a year ago, down slightly from 3.5% in June.
Lettuce prices plunged more than 16% last month after a recall of iceberg lettuce from Mexico, while falling gasoline and grocery prices offset rising rents and airfares.
Stripping out volatile food and energy prices, "core inflation" was 2.5% for the 12 months ending in July, down from 2.6% in June.
Market odds of a September rate hike fell below 40% after Wednesday's report, though gasoline prices remain more than a dollar higher than before the Iran-Strait of Hormuz conflict, according to AAA.
Easing inflation provides welcome news for the Federal Reserve, which has committed to controlling prices, though policymakers will review another inflation report before gathering next month.

summary: On Wednesday, NASA announced that astronaut Mike Fincke will leave the agency after 30 years of service, ending a career as a retired U.S. Air Force colonel.
Over his three-decade career, Fincke flew four missions, accumulating 549 days in orbit—the fourth highest among NASA colleagues—and completed nine spacewalks totaling 48 hours and 37 minutes.

Fincke's final mission, SpaceX Crew-11, ended early in January 2026 due to an undisclosed medical issue; NASA returned the crew early to access advanced medical imaging unavailable on the space station.

"After exactly 30 years, I am departing NASA, but I remain deeply committed to the work of exploration," Fincke said. Vanessa Wyche, director of NASA's Johnson Space Center, called his career "remarkable" and reflective of three decades of dedication.
He remains committed to goals like returning to the Moon and traveling to Mars, expressing excitement to "help prepare the next generation of engineers, explorers, and leaders.
title: NASA Astronaut Mike Fincke retires, logging 549 days in space

The White House cited ransomware and financial fraud as threats from foreign-based criminal organizations, prompting the administration to create a framework encouraging private firms to gather intelligence and propose cyber operations to address these threats.

Cyber effects includes the potential "manipulation, disruption, denial, degradation, or destruction of information systems, networks, physical or virtual infrastructure," according to the memo, defining the scope of operations participating companies may conduct.
Participating firms must maintain a $1 million bond or escrow to participate, with operations overseen by DHS and the Department of Justice under federal supervision and control.

summary: Montana State University opened a $10 million Wool Lab in July, a facility dedicated to making wool production more efficient and profitable for Montana sheep ranchers. Superintendent Brent Roeder manages the lab, which aims to revitalize the regional industry through research and innovation.

Over the last 80 years, the American sheep herd has decreased by 90% as synthetic fabrics overwhelmed the market. Roeder argues the industry suffered from years of economic neglect, requiring new investment to compete against cheaper imports.

Legislative appropriations and private industry donations funded the project. Stefanie Leach, executive assistant with the Montana Wool Growers Association, said the organization contributed $100,000, arguing the facility provides "necessary work" to foster innovation.

Roeder hopes the lab teaches students "why the wool industry is still important and relevant." Training the next generation is crucial for innovation, he emphasized, ensuring Montana sheep ranchers can compete long-term.

Sheep rancher Becky Weed, who utilized lab resources in the 1980s, noted modern producers need help processing and marketing their fiber. Weed observed that growers today must pay closer attention to market demand to succeed.
title: Montana State University Launches a New Wool Lab to Revive an Old Industry

The dispute stems from 1893, when Thomas Proctor acquired undeveloped land later sold at a 1908 tax sale, sparking a legal battle over natural gas rights valued at an estimated $1 billion.

Industry groups including the Marcellus Shale Coalition supported Act 27, arguing the 2025 ruling created unacceptable uncertainty for property owners, as the state estimates the law affects up to 1 million acres.

Challenging the new law, attorney Mark Aronchick argued it violates the Pennsylvania Constitution by retroactively changing property rules, while the family continues litigating three active cases against state agencies.

Courts are weighing next steps on the Game Commission's move to drop pending suits, while Judge Wallace criticized the rapid legislative process, noting the "third branch" must maintain its independence.

Council Speaker Julie Menin sent letters alleging "false, deceptive, unconscionable and objectionable marketing practices."

This inquiry follows a June Wall Street Journal investigation alleging Polymarket used content creators to simulate trades and create false impressions of profitability. The report found about 70% of promotional videos involved simulated activity rather than actual market trades.

Council Member Harvey Epstein, chair of the Committee on Consumer and Worker Protection, said the council has "a responsibility to investigate their claims and the advertising tactics these companies are using to ensure they are following the law."

summary: On Wednesday, the Congressional Budget Office raised its 2026 deficit forecast to $2.1 trillion, roughly $200 billion above its February projection, citing weaker-than-expected tariff and customs collections as the primary driver.

After the Supreme Court invalidated IEEPA tariff authority in February, the federal government refunded about $100 billion of $150 billion collected, shifting remaining duties to Section 122 and Section 301 authorities.

July spending reached $766 billion against $334 billion in revenue, while debt servicing is on track to exceed $1 trillion this year. Medicare spending and roughly $37.5 billion in war costs with Iran compounded the shortfall.

The deficit now equals about 6.6% of GDP, more than double Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent's 3% goal. Economist Alex Durante of the Tax Foundation said tariffs are "an unreliable long-term revenue source."

Section 122 and Section 301 tariff authorities now face ongoing court scrutiny, creating legal uncertainty for future revenue. Bessent argued administration policies will drive "trillions in new investment," yet analysts remain skeptical about offsetting structural losses.

summary: On Wednesday, the Justice Department unveiled criminal charges against 11 people, alleging they participated in an "extensive marriage fraud scheme" involving more than 1,000 sham marriages between Chinese nationals and United States citizens.

Foreign nationals paid facilitators as much as approximately $100,000 for assistance obtaining sham marriages, while recruiters paid United States citizens as much as $30,000 to participate in the scheme, according to the indictment.

To maintain the appearance of legitimacy, participants staged wedding ceremonies at restaurants wearing traditional attire and posed for photographs, which defendants then submitted to United States Citizenship and Immigration Services as evidence of genuine relationships.
Attorney General Todd Blanche described the operation as "one of the largest marriage fraud prosecutions in U.S. history," stating it showed "how far people will go to cheat our immigration system."

The announcement follows an executive order signed by President Donald Trump last week restricting "birth tourism," as the Justice Department and Homeland Security Investigations continue pursuing immigration fraud nationwide.

summary: On August 11, a NASA ensemble forecast predicted a coronal mass ejection's arrival at 10:32 UTC to the minute, matching the recorded shock arrival exactly while displaying a wide interval of uncertainty.
Analysts used solar-wind data from ACE and DSCOVR spacecraft near the Sun-Earth L1 point to identify the shock arrival boundary, a methodology that improves upon the 11-year accuracy record.

Findings published August 12 in Science Advances demonstrate the AstroRad vest could reduce radiation exposure by about 60% in solar storms as fierce as 1972 and nearly 40% during a calamity mirroring 1989.

Lead scientist Jordan Houri and his team analyzed high-fidelity data from manikins Zohar and Helga, confirming the vest shields vital organs and providing critical insights for future deep-space exploration.
Future moon bases and potential Mars missions will extend mission durations, driving up radiation risks and making the AstroRad vest essential for protecting astronauts during dangerous solar storms.
title: Radiation Vest Tested on NASA Moonshot Can Cut Astronauts’ Exposure in Solar Storms, Study Suggests

bias: Left-Leaning coverage foregrounds Lebanon ’s condemnation, repeatedly invoking “systematic destruction” and “serious violation” to portray Israel as responsible for extensive civilian harm, while de-emphasizing its military rationale.

Right-Leaning coverage also uses “destruction,” but pivots toward Lebanon’s claim that Israel’s justification “does not stand up to any logic,” emphasizing disputed military-facility claims, Lebanese army deployment, and residents’ return.
Center coverage juxtaposes both positions, attributing “systematic destruction” in quotation marks and noting possible legal violations.

summary: On Wednesday, Lebanon's National News Agency reported Israeli troops detonated civilian infrastructure in southern villages, including a municipal building, school, and health clinic in Zawtar al-Shariqya.

A June framework deal between Lebanon and Israel aimed to disarm Hezbollah and withdraw forces to 'pilot zones,' yet Israel Katz vowed Wednesday to maintain troops in a 'security zone' to destroy underground infrastructure.

Salam stated these "attacks, incursions, demolitions and the systematic destruction of homes" violate international law, rejecting claims that villages are "military facilities" as an excuse for displacing inhabitants.

General Joseph Clearfield met with Lebanese army chief Rodolphe Haykal and President Joseph Aoun on Wednesday to discuss security arrangements and the "difficulties the army faces" due to ongoing Israeli destruction.
Israel and Lebanon are scheduled to hold an eighth round of US-sponsored negotiations in Rome next month as both nations navigate the framework agreement's implementation amid persistent violence.
title: Lebanon Condemns Israel’s ‘Systematic Destruction’ in South as Violation of International Law

bias: Left-Leaning coverage frames a regulator’s inquiry through “alleged links,” cooperation, and the foundation’s prior serious-incident report, while right-leaning outlets use “sham organisation,” “bankrolling terror group,” and “under the guise of aid” to portray deliberate Hamas financing.
Center coverage bridges them, detailing alleged cash or humanitarian-supply transfers, concealed beneficiaries, and manipulated records or photographs.

Right reporting contrasts those claims with the foundation’s stated humanitarian, educational, religious, and welfare mission; across perspectives, evidence, defenses, and adjudication remain unclear.
All emphasize the Charity Commission inquiry and alleged Hamas connections, revealing tensions over aid, Muslim institutions, terrorism, and evidentiary caution.
summary: The Charity Commission launched a statutory inquiry yesterday into the Croydon-based Al-Khair Foundation to investigate alleged links to Hamas . Regulators are assessing whether trustees exercised adequate due diligence on partners and the use of funds.

Following the July 31 arrest of Turkish national Mohammad Yousef Hasna, Counter Terror Policing London executed two search warrants at addresses in Croydon. Prosecutors allege Hasna conspired to funnel money and supplies to Hamas through a sham humanitarian organization.

Hasna, 45, faces United States charges of conspiring to finance terrorism, with each count carrying a maximum 20-year prison sentence. The Al-Khair Foundation is subject to a legal order restricting certain financial transactions without Charity Commission consent.
The Al-Khair Foundation stated it is "co-operating fully" with the inquiry and maintains that Hasna is not an employee but works with one of its global partners to deliver aid in Gaza.

Reporting more than £74 million in income for the financial year ending July 31, 2025, the foundation's substantial revenue underscores the inquiry's significance. Regulators must determine whether trustees conducted proper due diligence on partners and charitable resource allocation.
title: UK Charity Probed Over Hamas Financing Links
Questions about Sydney protest spark tense exchange at royal commission

bias: Left-Leaning coverage foregrounds human hardship: a roughly 5,000-sailor crew, family concerns, alleged attempts to jump overboard, and an Iran-war extension, using phrases such as “breaking point” and “urgent action.” Right-leaning coverage emphasizes congressional accountability, particularly Democrats’ “demand” for an “inquiry,” while describing “poor conditions” and “mental-health crises.” Center coverage is more restrained, stressing over 200 days without coming ashore, a possible consecutive-days-at-sea record, and growing “anxiety,” with attention to supplies, plumbing, and water.

Across perspectives, the prolonged deployment, shortages, infrastructure problems, and crew welfare prompt concern, reflecting differing priorities of human impact, oversight, and institutional scrutiny.
summary: Senator Richard Blumenthal demanded the Navy account for conditions aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln, which "has been deployed more than 250 days" without coming ashore in over 200 days, setting a consecutive-days-at-sea record.

Senator Ruben Gallego called for "an official oversight visit" to investigate reported alarming conditions, with the USS Abraham Lincoln having departed San Diego on November 21, 2025, for a Middle East deployment.

Blumenthal cited "widespread reports of shortages of basic supplies, water contamination, plumbing issues, deteriorating mental health, deck safety concerns" aboard the carrier, where sailors and Marines endure grueling 12- to 16-hour shifts with no days off.

Family members of the 5,000 sailors and Marines clashed with Navy leadership over difficult conditions in recent meetings, demanding to know when loved ones would return home; the Navy did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Congressional Democrats questioned the deployment's management, with critics labeling the treatment of service members "disgusting" and "dangerous" amid the ongoing Middle East mission that began following US-Israeli actions against Iran on February 28.
title: Senators Demand Inquiry Into Conditions Aboard USS Abraham Lincoln

summary: On Tuesday, August 11, 2026, Scott Jensen and Zack Filipovich won their respective primary elections, securing spots on the November ballot for Minnesota State Auditor.
Incumbent Julie Blaha announced last year she would not seek re-election, prompting the race for a new State Auditor overseeing roughly $60 billion in local spending across Minnesota.

Jensen, a former state senator and family doctor, defeated GOP-endorsed Braham Mayor Nate George and Will Finn, holding about 67% of the vote with about 73% of precincts reporting shortly after 10 p.m.

Filipovich, a former Duluth City Council member, secured the DFL nomination running unopposed, bringing experience as an Air Force combat veteran and Director of Licensing & Investigations for the Mille Lacs Band of Ojibwe.

The incoming State Auditor will manage an operating budget of around $20.4 million, serve on the State Board of Investment, and oversee financial activity across 3,300 local governments for an annual salary of $137,358.
title: Filipovich, Jensen appear to be headed to November ballot for Minnesota auditor

summary: Following a 'national energy emergency' declared last year by President Donald Trump , the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers is fast-tracking the expansion of the Plaquemines LNG terminal in Louisiana.

The agency cut the public comment period to 10 days, allowing the facility to double in size from nearly 590 acres to about 1,220 while increasing production capacity from 1.4 trillion to around 2.3 trillion cubic feet of gas annually.

With Plaquemines Parish losing more than 250 square miles of land over the past 60 years, environmentalists warn the project could damage up to 470 acres of wetlands in a region already suffering from a coastal crisis.

Healthy Gulf senior policy director Matt Rota noted the facility is permitted to release 8.1 million tons of greenhouse gases annually, stating, 'Destroying 400 more acres in Plaquemines Parish is ridiculous.'

Critics like Griffin Bird, a research analyst with the Environmental Integrity Project, question how the expansion helps domestic energy independence, despite arguments from local leaders that it will spur economic activity.
title: Trump’s ‘energy emergency’ could fast-track massive expansion of Plaquemines LNG export terminal

bias: Left-Leaning coverage frames the lawsuit as a political “scandal,” calling Miller “embattled” and the disclosure “incomprehensible recklessness,” while stressing abuse allegations and potential damage to his congressional seat.
Center coverage de-emphasizes that wider crisis, repeatedly portraying the image as an “accidental release” and foregrounding legal attribution.

Right-Leaning coverage instead highlights alleged federal intimate-image violations, the restraining-order request, and vivid claims involving a gun and hot water, using “another legal battle” and “nude photo” to intensify the stakes.
All perspectives emphasize the lawsuit, the two-year-old child, and the Dropbox disclosure, reflecting competing priorities of political accountability, procedural caution, and legal-moral alarm.
summary: On Wednesday, Emily Moreno filed a federal civil-rights lawsuit against Representative Max Miller, attorney Aaron Minc, and Minc LLC, alleging they recklessly published an unredacted nude photograph of her two-year-old daughter.

During a live broadcast on Twitter on August 2, Miller distributed a public Dropbox link, urging viewers to "take a look at the documents" containing an unredacted PDF with the child's genitalia and name exposed more than 70 times.

Minc initially configured the Dropbox folder with public editor permissions, and the intimate image remained accessible online for about 23 hours before removal. A pediatrician confirmed the photo depicts genitalia, contradicting Minc's media claims the child was partially clothed.

The filing asserts federal claims under 15 U.S.C. § 6851, seeking $150,000 in statutory damages per disclosure, plus attorney fees and injunctive relief. The lawsuit also alleges state-law violations including civil liability for criminal acts and invasion of privacy.

After initial viewers deleted files, Minc restored the folder under pressure, republishing the unredacted image; Miller then rebroadcast the link. Both defendants have refused requests for download logs, blocking assessment of the image's full exposure.
title: Emily Moreno sues Rep. Max Miller, alleging he posted nude photo of daughter

bias: Left-Leaning coverage frames Trump’s plane switch as reckless deception, stressing “unwitting decoys,” a “shell game,” and claims he “lied,” while emphasizing reporters and officials allegedly endangered for his protection.

Right-Leaning coverage pivots toward national-security drama, invoking a “secret jet,” Iranian “threat,” “bait,” and even a “death jet,” portraying the press as vulnerable and the operation as possibly necessary, though unexplained.
A pivotal divide is whether the aircraft was deliberate bait or also involved a minor electrical problem—de-emphasized on the left.
Center coverage mostly recounts the sequence and anonymous sourcing.
All agree on the covert transfer, passengers left behind, and unresolved security questions, reflecting broader distrust over presidential accountability versus threat-focused defense.
summary: Following the NATO summit in Ankara, Turkey, President Donald Trump covertly swapped aircraft using a catering truck, leaving Air Force One to serve as a decoy while he flew separately on a government jet.

U.S. officials initiated the maneuver after intelligence indicated a potential surface-to-air missile threat against the president's aircraft, prompting security teams to protect him during departure from the region.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent remained aboard the decoy aircraft with press corps members, who were instructed to keep window shades closed while unaware of the threat.
On Tuesday, Trump defended the secret flight swap, telling reporters the military and Secret Service made the decision and claiming the maneuver was necessary for "equal safety."

Once in England, the administration executed a second maneuver to restore appearances that Trump had traveled on the decoy plane, sparking criticism over prioritizing security over journalistic transparency.
title: Rubio and Bessent Stayed on Decoy Flight From Turkey as Trump Switched Planes, Official Says

bias: Left-Leaning coverage foregrounds the alleged racial motive—“targeting Black people”—and describes Gillum as “quietly released,” inviting concern about transparency while retaining legal qualifiers like “accused.” Right-leaning coverage foregrounds the threat and his former occupation, using “ex-cop,” “mass-shooting plot,” and “attack” to evoke law-and-order concerns, while stressing that he was released and not indicted.
Center coverage adds procedural context, including the June grand-jury action and potential 15-year terrorism sentence.

summary: A Louisiana grand jury in June declined to indict 45-year-old former police officer Christopher Gillum on state terrorism charges, leading to his release from custody.

On April 22, 2026, Okaloosa County deputies arrested Gillum at a Destin, Florida, hotel with a handgun and approximately 200 rounds of ammunition after he allegedly planned to drive to New Orleans to conduct a mass shooting.

Several jurisdictional issues complicated the case because Gillum never entered Louisiana before his arrest, and Louisiana's statute for "terrorizing" requires that a crime of violence be imminent or in progress.

Following the grand jury decision, Gillum's family took him "to a treatment facility out of the state," according to Louisiana Attorney General Liz Murrill's office, and he faces no additional criminal charges elsewhere.

Former FBI executive Katherine Schweit noted that thwarted acts of mass violence do not always lead to indictments because "it's very difficult to convince a jury" when no act occurs; the investigation involved federal and state authorities across Louisiana, North Carolina, and Florida.
title: Ex-officer accused of plotting New Orleans attack is released after grand jury declines to indict

All agree on Hegseth’s announcement, anti-drug aims, coalition participation, and the Panama setting, reflecting shared concern over narcotics but divergent views of intervention and regional power.
summary: On Wednesday, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced that Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella requested joint U.S. military operations "to destroy terrorists and terror networks."
During a Panama meeting of the Americas Counter-Cartel Coalition, Hegseth confirmed Colombia is joining the "Shield of the Americas" initiative as its 19th member.
The State Department announced last week a $1 billion military aid package to "support the De la Espriella Administration" in defeating narcoterrorist organizations threatening regional security.

Senator Ivan Cepeda of the opposition Historic Pact party rejected the announcement, citing constitutional requirements for Senate approval and claiming the president wants to "surrender our government, our territory and our sovereignty."

Separately, Hegseth urged the nearly 20 countries in attendance to reject the International Criminal Court, arguing U.S. operations remain legal under international humanitarian law and should not strip governments of their "sovereignty.
title: Hegseth Says Colombia's New President Has Requested US Collaboration in Anti-Drug Efforts
